claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening under the relevant irradiation conditions.
Increasing the V content from 11 at% to approximately 15 at% will inhibit radiation-induced precipitation.
Increasing the V content to approximately 15 at% will preserve negligible irradiation hardening.
Increasing the V content to approximately 15 at% will enhance suitability for bulk fabrication.
Increased V will modify the local atomic environment.
Increased V will stabilize grain boundaries.
Increased V will reduce diffusion pathways that facilitate precipitate nucleation.
Increased V will improve sintering behavior for bulk processing.
Increasing V enhances irradiation-defect sink efficiency by changing the local free-energy landscape and elastic strain fields near grain boundaries.
The V-induced changes will impede radiation-induced segregation and clustering responsible for precipitation.
At approximately 8 dpa, the V-enhanced alloy will have a lower radiation-induced precipitate density than the unmodified alloy.
At approximately 8 dpa, the V-enhanced alloy will have smaller radiation-induced precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
At approximately 8 dpa, the V-enhanced alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
The V-enhanced alloy will exhibit improved densification during bulk fabrication.
Unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops radiation-induced precipitation at approximately 8 dpa.
Unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
The proposed behavior applies up to approximately 8 dpa over 500–700°C, provided that the nanocrystalline structure is retained.
